## Quantitative Calibration {#sec-calibration}

The calibration maps the model parameters to the AI infrastructure sector using publicly available data from company filings, industry reports, and the scaling laws literature. The calibration is *stylized*: the goal is to discipline the model's quantitative magnitudes and illustrate cross-sectional heterogeneity, not to structurally estimate firm-level primitives or test the model empirically. I flag two caveats at the outset. First, the Leland default framework is an analytically tractable approximation to financial distress risk. It fits public-debt issuers better than VC-backed labs, though the qualitative predictions apply across financing structures (see @sec-discussion). The Leland setting is becoming more literal as AI labs mature: OpenAI secured a \$4B revolving credit facility in October 2024,^[\url{https://www.cnbc.com/2024/10/03/openai-gets-4-billion-revolving-credit-line-on-top-of-latest-funding.html}.] and xAI arranged \$5B+ in secured notes and term loans (sourced in Internet Appendix C). Press reports place 2025 hyperscaler bond issuance at \$121B. Second, the training fractions $\hat{\phi}$ are inferred from incomplete data and carry substantial uncertainty ($\pm 0.10$). I set the demand process parameters first, then the technology and cost parameters, and then the four stylized firm archetypes; the last two subsections report the baseline solution and its sensitivity to the parameters. @tbl-parameters in the Internet Appendix summarizes the calibration status of each parameter.

### Demand Process

The demand process parameters govern the drift and volatility of AI compute demand under each regime. I use regime-dependent drifts $\mu_L = 0.01$ and $\mu_H = 0.06$, with common volatility $\sigma = 0.25$. The L-regime drift captures baseline growth in cloud computing revenue; the H-regime drift is meant to capture the substantially higher growth that would characterize a world in which transformative AI capabilities generate large new demand. Both drifts are *risk-adjusted* (certainty-equivalent) growth rates, not observed revenue growth: the cloud revenue growth of 24--39\% cited in @tbl-sources in the Internet Appendix is consistent with a much lower $\mu_H$ once the substantial risk premium embedded in $r$ is netted out, and the convergence requirement $r > \mu_H$ bounds the admissible value from above. Because the implied risk adjustment cannot be measured directly, $\mu_H = 0.06$ is best read as a disciplined choice rather than an empirical estimate; @tbl-parameters in the Internet Appendix records its status as "Chosen". The common volatility $\sigma = 0.25$ is a chosen proxy rather than a measured moment: the demand shifter $X$ is a latent risk-adjusted state variable, and its closest observable analogue (quarterly revenue growth of cloud providers) is smoothed by multi-year contracts and revenue-recognition rules, so that analogue disciplines the order of magnitude without identifying $\sigma$, which @tbl-parameters in the Internet Appendix likewise lists as "Chosen". The interior-capacity condition (A2) discussed below admits $\sigma \in (0.19, 0.39)$ at the baseline values of the remaining parameters, and $\sigma = 0.25$ sits inside that window.

The arrival rate $\lambda = 0.10$ per year implies an expected time to regime switch of 10 years. This baseline represents a moderate prior, intended to approximate the marginal investor's belief rather than any particular executive's view. It is more conservative than the beliefs implied by @amodei2024machines ($\lambda \approx 0.30$--$0.50$), and it sits at the lower endpoint of the range implied by Hassabis's public statements ($\lambda \approx 0.10$--$0.15$); the dispersion across these views generates the cross-sectional variation in investment behavior analyzed in @sec-valuation.

I set the baseline discount rate to $r = 0.12$, a risk-adjusted WACC chosen to represent a frontier AI lab rather than measured for one. As discussed in @sec-model ([Footnote \ref{fn:wacc}]{.content-visible when-format="pdf"}[the footnote on risk-adjusted discounting]{.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}), $r$ is the WACC and $\mu_s$ is the risk-adjusted growth rate (the physical drift minus an appropriate risk premium, so that discounting expected cash flows at $r$ yields the correct present value); all valuation uses this reduced-form framework. The baseline exceeds typical corporate WACCs because frontier AI labs carry substantial technology risk and are typically high-growth with elevated cost of equity. Industry estimates give WACCs of 7.2\% for computer software and 10.8\% for semiconductors,^[\url{https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/datafile/wacc.htm}.] and, assuming betas of 1.5--2.5 for comparable listed firms, the CAPM implies a cost of equity of roughly 10.5--15.0\%. The analytical results and figures in @sec-model use $r = 0.12$ throughout; these illustrate model properties at a representative WACC and do not correspond to any specific firm archetype. The firm-specific WACCs in @tbl-firms (ranging from 0.10 to 0.18) play a narrower role than a full cross-sectional sensitivity analysis would. The interior-capacity condition (A2), $1/\gamma < (\beta_H - 1)/(\alpha\beta_H) < 1$, depends on $r$ through the characteristic root $\beta_H$, and at the baseline values of the remaining parameters it admits only $r \in (0.097, 0.135)$. The Google-like hyperscaler ($r = 0.10$) and the baseline ($r = 0.12$) lie inside this window; the OpenAI-like platform ($r = 0.14$), the Anthropic-like frontier lab ($r = 0.15$), and the xAI-like compute racer ($r = 0.18$) violate its upper bound. When that bound fails the capacity problem has no interior optimum, because the option-value factor diverges as $K \to 0$, so the solvers verify (A2) before optimizing and raise an error rather than report a boundary artifact (Internet Appendix B). Archetype-specific WACCs accordingly enter the analysis through one channel only: the capacity-free training-allocation inversion $\lambda = (\hat{\phi}/(1-\hat{\phi}))^{1-\alpha}(r - \mu_H)$ reported later in this section. Every trigger and capacity result in the paper is computed at the baseline WACC, and the sensitivity sweeps vary $r$ inside the admissible window.

### Technology Parameters

The revenue elasticity $\alpha = 0.40$ governs diminishing returns to capacity in revenue generation, entering both the L-regime inference contest (@eq-contest-L) and the H-regime training contest (@eq-contest-H). The compute-to-loss power laws in @kaplan2020scaling and @hoffmann2022training motivate a concave revenue technology, but they do not measure $\alpha$: a loss exponent is not a revenue elasticity, and no public series maps compute to revenue at the firm level. I therefore treat $\alpha = 0.40$ as a chosen value (@tbl-parameters in the Internet Appendix). Holding contest share fixed (or in the single-firm case), doubling the relevant capacity measure increases revenue by approximately $2^{0.4} \approx 1.32$ times, a 32\% increase rather than 100\%, which is the signature of diminishing returns to scale. In a symmetric duopoly, a unilateral doubling also raises the contest share, so the total revenue gain is larger (approximately 50\% at baseline). This choice carries two limitations. First, condition (A2) admits only $\alpha \in (0.356, 0.534)$ at the baseline values of the remaining parameters, so $\alpha = 0.40$ sits close to the lower bound; numerical optimization does not relax the restriction, because the joint optimization over $(\log K, \phi)$ verifies (A2) first and raises an error when it fails, so all sensitivity ranges are truncated to the admissible window (Internet Appendix B). Second, the trigger and capacity are highly sensitive to $\alpha$ within that window, with elasticities of $+19.7$ and $+24.2$ (@tbl-elasticities in the Internet Appendix), which is why the paper reports ratios and percentage differences rather than levels, and why the archetype table below is read as an illustrative cross-section rather than as a set of firm-level primitives. The cost function $I(K) = cK^\gamma$ with convexity $\gamma = 1.50$ captures increasing marginal costs from power constraints, supply chain bottlenecks (particularly for advanced GPUs), and site preparation costs; I normalize the unit cost $c = 1.0$, so all monetary values are interpreted relative to this normalization.

The operating cost rate $\delta = 0.03$ represents the ongoing cost of maintaining installed capacity (power, cooling, maintenance, and personnel), expressed as a fraction of capacity per year, distinct from both accounting depreciation and economic depreciation of GPU hardware. Data center equipment is typically depreciated over a 3--5 year useful life, implying accounting depreciation of 20--33\% per year, and power costs alone can reach \$0.05--0.10/kWh at hyperscale. In the model, the *capital* cost of hardware is captured in $cK^\gamma$; $\delta$ captures only the *operating* flow cost. Economic depreciation through technological obsolescence (e.g., H100$\to$B200 transitions) would justify a higher effective $\delta$. Nothing substantive turns on the choice. Because $\delta$ enters only through the total cost $b(K) = \delta K/r + cK^\gamma$ and revenue is a pure power of capacity, a change in $\delta$ is exactly equivalent to a rescaling of the capacity unit: replacing $(\delta, K)$ by $(\delta s^{1-\gamma}, K/s)$ leaves the optimization problem unchanged up to a constant factor. The elasticities of $+2.2$ for the trigger and $+2.0$ for capacity in @tbl-elasticities in the Internet Appendix are exactly the exponents of that rescaling, $(\gamma - \alpha)/(\gamma - 1)$ and $1/(\gamma - 1)$, rather than economic sensitivity. Recomputing the model at $\delta = 0.10$ confirms this: the levels move ($X^*$ from $0.0047$ to $0.0667$, $K^*$ from $0.0067$ to $0.0747$), while $\phi^* = 0.70$, the trigger ratio $X_P / X_L^{\text{mono}} = 0.57$, the follower-to-leader capacity ratio, and the Dario's dilemma losses (26.2\% conservative versus 5.6\% aggressive) are numerically identical to their baseline values. The chosen $\delta$ is therefore part of the cost normalization rather than a separately identified quantity. That is also why the industry operating-cost estimates in @tbl-sources in the Internet Appendix, an annual burden of 30--40\% of hardware capital expenditure, do not contradict $\delta = 0.03$: the model's $\delta$ is a flow per unit of the abstract capacity index $K$, whose scale is fixed by the normalization $c = 1$, not per dollar of installed hardware. The one class of reported quantities that is not invariant in this sense is the credit spreads and default probabilities of @sec-valuation, which are evaluated at a fixed $(X, K)$ rather than at the optimal policy.

### Stylized Firm Archetypes

I construct four stylized firm archetypes representing the major categories of frontier AI labs. These archetypes are designed to span the relevant cross-sectional variation in investment intensity, leverage, and training allocation; they are *illustrative composites*, not structural estimates of any specific company's parameters.

| Calibration input | Frontier Lab | Platform | Hyperscaler | Compute Racer |
|:----------|:------------|:---------|:------------|:--------------|
| Reference firm (illustrative) | Anthropic-like | OpenAI-like | Google-like | xAI-like |
| Revenue 2024 (\$B) | 0.9 | 3.7 | 43.0 | 0.2 |
| Revenue 2025 (\$B) | 4.5 | 12.5 | 60.0 | 0.5 |
| CapEx 2025 (\$B) | 3.0 | 12.0 | 91.0 | 10.0 |
| CapEx / Revenue | 0.67 | 0.96 | 1.52 | 20.0 |
| Leverage (debt / total capital) | 0.05 | 0.05 | 0.10 | 0.15 |
| WACC (per year) | 0.15 | 0.14 | 0.10 | 0.18 |
| Training fraction $\hat{\phi}$ | 0.55 | 0.60 | 0.35 | 0.75 |

: Stylized firm archetypes: calibration inputs. Revenue covers AI-related activities; CapEx includes cloud compute commitments (Anthropic-like and OpenAI-like archetypes) and total infrastructure spending (Google-like and xAI-like archetypes). $\hat{\phi}$ is the observed training fraction assigned to each archetype and is distinct from the model's endogenous training fraction $\phi$; its values are set from executive statements [@amodei2026dwarkesh], the Epoch AI compute analysis, and Deloitte's TMT Predictions 2026. All values are order-of-magnitude composites, not precise calibrations. {#tbl-firms tbl-colwidths="[24,15,15,15,15]"}

The values in @tbl-firms are approximate composites derived from public filings (10-K, 10-Q), earnings call guidance, press reports, and analyst estimates; Internet Appendix C documents the sourcing archetype by archetype and @tbl-sources there lists the underlying sources. Each archetype's revenue entry covers AI-related activities rather than diversified corporate totals, but the concept behind that label differs across archetypes: segment revenue for the Google-like hyperscaler, firm-wide AI revenue for the other three. For the two archetypes modelled on privately held firms (Anthropic-like and xAI-like), the values rest on press reports and carry lower confidence than publicly disclosed data; they should be read as order-of-magnitude inputs. Because the revenue and CapEx concepts are not harmonized across the four archetypes (sector revenue versus segment revenue, cloud commitments versus owned infrastructure), the columns of @tbl-firms should be read one at a time as inputs to the model, not compared with each other as measured cross-sectional moments; the discussion below therefore describes the archetypes as design choices rather than as measured dispersion. The ratios and percentage differences the paper reports are robust to moderate perturbation of these inputs within the admissible parameter region; the levels of $X^*$ and $K^*$ are not (@tbl-elasticities in the Internet Appendix; Internet Appendix E).

The training fraction $\hat{\phi}$ values represent the approximate share of compute allocated to model training rather than to inference serving. They are inherently uncertain, because firms do not publicly disclose precise training-inference breakdowns. I triangulate the entries in @tbl-firms from three types of evidence: executive statements, the only firm-level compute decomposition with primary documentation that I could locate (Epoch AI's analysis of OpenAI's 2024 spend), and industry-wide trajectory estimates. Internet Appendix C sets out each in detail. The xAI-like compute racer allocates the most to training ($\hat{\phi} = 0.75$), consistent with a strategy of dedicating owned compute (the Colossus supercluster) to frontier model training while outsourcing inference to cloud providers.^[\url{https://x.com/elonmusk/status/1947701807389515912}.] The Google-like hyperscaler allocates the least ($\hat{\phi} = 0.35$), which is meant to capture the need to serve inference to billions of users across Search, Gmail, and YouTube; Google's seventh-generation Ironwood TPU is designed for inference workloads. The Anthropic-like and OpenAI-like archetypes fall between these extremes. These values carry substantial uncertainty, plausibly $\pm 0.10$ for each archetype, and should be read as order-of-magnitude discipline rather than as precise moments for structural identification. The moderate elasticity of $\phi^*$ with respect to $\lambda$ ($\varepsilon \approx +0.5$ at baseline, reflecting $\varepsilon_{\phi^*,\lambda} = (1-\phi^*)/(1-\alpha)$) means that $\phi^*$ varies slowly with $\lambda$, so the inverse mapping $\lambda(\hat{\phi})$ is steep: modest uncertainty in the observed training fraction ($\pm 0.10$) translates into a wide range of implied arrival rates. Inverting the closed-form allocation FOC, $\lambda = (\hat{\phi}/(1-\hat{\phi}))^{1-\alpha}(r - \mu_H)$, for each archetype at $\hat{\phi} \pm 0.10$ yields implied arrival rates that span roughly a factor of two (e.g., the xAI-like archetype implies $\lambda \in [0.09, 0.17]$, corresponding to expected horizons of 6--11 years, while the Google-like hyperscaler implies $\lambda \in [0.03, 0.05]$, or 19--32 years). I attach two qualifications to this inversion. First, it holds the discount rate at the common baseline $r = 0.12$; because the implied $\lambda$ scales with $r - \mu_H$, using archetype-specific WACCs would shift the levels materially (the xAI-like archetype at $r = 0.18$ implies $\lambda \in [0.17, 0.34]$, while the Google-like archetype at $r = 0.10$ implies $\lambda \in [0.02, 0.04]$), in this case widening rather than narrowing the cross-sectional dispersion. Second, the ordering claim should be read as applying to common perturbations of the $\hat{\phi}$ values: the baseline ordering xAI-like $>$ OpenAI-like $>$ Anthropic-like $>$ Google-like in implied $\lambda$ is preserved when all $\hat{\phi}$ shift together, but the $\pm 0.10$ bands of adjacent archetypes overlap, so independent errors could reorder neighboring pairs (though not the endpoints). The cross-sectional variation ($\hat{\phi}$ ranging from 0.35 to 0.75) is more informative than any individual value.

The boundary between "training" and "inference" is also blurring. Inference-time scaling (chain-of-thought reasoning, search-augmented generation, and agentic workflows) uses inference hardware to produce capability improvements that were previously achievable only through training.^[\url{https://x.com/polynoamial/status/1834280425457426689}.] The model treats $\hat{\phi}$ as a fixed allocation at investment time; in practice, firms dynamically reallocate GPUs between training and inference on timescales of weeks (see @sec-discussion for the direction of bias from this simplification).

The archetypes are constructed to differ along three dimensions. The first is investment intensity: the xAI-like compute racer commits 20.0 times its revenue, a setting meant to capture a strategy of building training clusters ahead of monetization, while the Google-like hyperscaler commits 1.52 times revenue and the Anthropic-like and OpenAI-like archetypes sit closer to parity. The second is leverage, which is low by construction throughout: the two archetypes modelled on private labs are effectively all-equity funded ($\ell = 0.05$), and even the hyperscaler carries only modest debt ($\ell = 0.10$). This low-leverage structure is meant to capture the venture-backed financing of AI labs and the availability of equity capital at high valuations; were these firms to mature and take on traditional debt (revolving credit facilities, secured notes, data center ABS), leverage ratios would rise toward the Leland framework's domain.^[The leverage ratios in @tbl-firms are round assumptions informed by qualitative evidence rather than measured market-value debt-to-capital ratios, which none of the private archetypes publishes: Anthropic is effectively all-equity; OpenAI secured a \$4B revolving credit facility; Alphabet carries modest net debt; xAI arranged \$5B+ in secured notes and term loans (\url{https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-09/musk-s-xai-reports-higher-quarterly-loss-plans-to-power-optimus}). They should be read with the same order-of-magnitude caveat as the other firm-level inputs.] The third is the training fraction, which varies by approximately a factor of two across archetypes (0.35 to 0.75) and is consistent with different business models and different beliefs about where the returns to AI compute investment are highest. Dispersion along these three dimensions is what drives the heterogeneous investment behavior analyzed in @sec-valuation.

### Baseline Results

Under the baseline calibration, the single-firm model with training-inference allocation produces an investment trigger $X^* \approx 0.0047$, capacity $K^* \approx 0.0067$, and training fraction $\phi^* \approx 0.70$, where the effective revenue coefficient $A_{\text{eff}}$ (@eq-a-eff) combines L-regime inference value and H-regime training value. By the solution convention discussed after Proposition 1, the duopoly leader's unconstrained (monopoly) policy coincides with this single-firm optimum, so $X_L^{\text{mono}} = X^* \approx 0.0047$. The duopoly equilibrium with zero leverage produces a follower policy of $X_F^* \approx 0.12$, $K_F \approx 0.26$, and $\phi_F^* \approx 0.70$, with the leader preempting at $X_P \approx 0.0027$. The large difference in scale between the leader ($K^* \approx 0.0067$) and the follower ($K_F \approx 0.26$, a factor of $38$) arises because the follower's contest share rises with its own capacity, so its effective elasticity of revenue to capacity is $\alpha(2 - s_F) \approx 0.48$ rather than $\alpha = 0.40$, and the capacity closed form is highly elastic at the baseline; the follower correspondingly delays entry to a demand level roughly $44$ times the preemption trigger, where the larger commitment is justified. @sec-duopoly discusses what this asymmetry does and does not say about AI rivalry, and Internet Appendix B verifies the wedge decomposition.

Because $c = 1$ fixes the cost scale by normalization (the same rescaling argument that makes the chosen $\delta$ part of the normalization rather than a separately identified quantity), the levels of $K$ and $X$ are not interpretable as physical units, and the quantitative content resides in *ratios* and *percentages*: the trigger ratio $X_P / X_L^{\text{mono}} \approx 0.57$ (conditional on the leader-scale convention; Internet Appendix B), the training fraction $\phi^* \approx 0.70$, the value-loss asymmetry (26\% versus 6\%), and the leverage gradient of credit spreads and default probabilities (@sec-valuation). To map to observable units one would set $c$ so that $I(K) = cK^\gamma$ matches observed CapEx for a given archetype. Setting $c \approx \$23\text{B}$, for example, maps the duopoly follower's investment cost $I(K_F) = K_F^{1.5} \approx 0.13$ to approximately \$3B, the Anthropic-like archetype's annual CapEx. Rescaling $c$ in this way affects no ratio, percentage, or spread reported in the paper.

Strategic interaction accelerates investment: the preemption discount is 43\%, with a preemption trigger of $X_P \approx 0.0027$ against the monopolist benchmark $X_L^{\text{mono}} \approx 0.0047$. Both firms optimally allocate approximately 70\% to training ($\phi^* \approx 0.70$), which follows from the high value of the H-regime continuation payoff at the baseline arrival rate $\lambda = 0.10$ and from the role invariance established in Proposition 3(ii).

### Sensitivity Analysis

The following comparative statics are robust across the calibration range; @tbl-elasticities in the Internet Appendix reports elasticities at the baseline. Higher volatility $\sigma$ increases the option value of waiting and raises the investment trigger, the standard real-options result that uncertainty raises the value of flexibility. Within the model, then, greater uncertainty about future demand would justify more cautious investment timing. A higher discount rate $r$ reduces the present value of future cash flows through $A_{\text{eff}}$, but it also raises the characteristic root $\beta_H$ and so lowers the option premium ratio $\beta_H/(\beta_H - 1)$. At baseline the second effect dominates, so a higher $r$ lowers both the trigger and optimal capacity. The archetype WACCs span 10\%--18\%, but condition (A2) admits only $r \in (0.097, 0.135)$, so the comparative static is evaluated over that narrower window; within it, the model implies materially different investment policies for firms holding identical beliefs about $\lambda$. Higher $\lambda$ increases the weight on H-regime revenue in $A_{\text{eff}}$ (@eq-a-eff), raising the effective revenue coefficient, lowering the investment trigger, and shifting the optimal training fraction $\phi^*$ upward as the expected payoff from training quality increases. Higher $\lambda$ therefore produces earlier investment and a larger training fraction, while single-firm $K^*$ is independent of $\lambda$ by Proposition 1 and the duopoly equilibrium capacity can differ through the contest function. In the model, more optimistic firms invest earlier and allocate more compute to frontier model development. Finally, lower revenue elasticity $\alpha$ (stronger diminishing returns) reduces optimal capacity sharply, and because the smaller installation is correspondingly cheaper to build and to operate, a lower $\alpha$ lowers the trigger as well. Both elasticities are large and positive ($+24.2$ for capacity and $+19.7$ for the trigger; @tbl-elasticities in the Internet Appendix), so at $\alpha = 0.38$ the trigger falls to $X^* \approx 0.0015$ and at $\alpha = 0.45$ it rises to $X^* \approx 0.038$, against the baseline $0.0047$. The firm with stronger diminishing returns therefore invests earlier but at a much smaller scale. This parameter also shapes the contest function: over the admissible range at and below the baseline, lower $\alpha$ reduces the benefit of capacity dominance in both regimes and weakens the preemption incentive, with the trigger ratio $X_P/X_L^{\text{mono}}$ rising from $0.57$ at $\alpha = 0.40$ to $0.60$ at $\alpha = 0.37$.
